name: Hausa city-states
summary: Walled trading cities of northern Nigeria, such as Kano and Katsina, famous for textiles and leather, until they became part of the Sokoto Caliphate (1804–1808).

knownFor.label: Kofar Mata dye pits
knownFor.note: Indigo dye pits in Kano, said to date from 1498.

knownFor.label: Queen Amina of Zazzau
knownFor.note: A warrior queen remembered in legend.

knownFor.label: Kano city walls
knownFor.note: Earth walls around the ancient city.

location.value: Between the Niger River and Lake Chad, in modern northern Nigeria. Southern Niger is not mentioned in the part read.

terrain.value: Savanna plains in northern Nigeria, cut by seasonal rivers.

climate.value: Tropical, with a long dry season and a short rainy season.

resources.value: Farmland, cotton, indigo, leather and salt.

disasters.value: Droughts and famines were recurring problems.

urbanisation.value: Walled cities such as Kano, Katsina and Zaria were centres of trade and craft.

disease.value: No reliable records survive; epidemics and famines likely struck periodically.

migration.value: Traders and scholars came from North Africa.

economicBase.value: Farming was the traditional livelihood; the main exports were leather, gold, cloth, salt, kola nuts, slaves and henna.

tradeRoutes.value: Trans-Saharan trade; kola nuts from the forest.

wealth.value: Trading cities grew wealthy from textiles, leather and caravan trade.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowrie shells and cloth strips were used as money.

inequality.value: A gap between rulers, merchants, farmers and enslaved people.

governmentType.value: The Hausa Bakwai were the seven “true” states and the Banza Bakwai the “illegitimate” ones; administration ran under the supervision of a sarki (king). The page does not call them independent city-states. Bornu vassalised the Hausa states, they were mostly tributary to Songhai, and Usman dan Fodio conquered them by 1808 into the Sokoto Caliphate.

keyRulers.value: Kano: Yaji I (reigned 1349–85), thought to be the first Kano ruler to convert to Islam; Muhammad Rumfa (1463–99). Katsina: Ibrahim Maje (1549–66).

succession.value: Royal families, with the ruler (sarki) chosen from a limited group.

institutions.value: Islamic law in later centuries; court officials.

eliteConflict.value: Palace rivalries and tension between the rulers and Muslim scholars.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry with quilted armour and mail, and mud walls around cities.

majorWars.value: The Sokoto jihad (1804–1808) under Usman dan Fodio overthrew most Hausa kingdoms; the page does not mention wars with Songhai, Bornu or Kebbi.

alliancesRivals.value: The cities sometimes paid tribute to Bornu or Songhai.

scienceEducation.value: Islamic scholarship and writing in Hausa with Arabic letters (Ajami).

openness.value: Open to traders from across the Sahara and West Africa.

communicationTransport.value: Caravans of donkeys and camels linked the cities to the Sahara and the south.

religion.value: Islam was widespread in the Hausa states by the 14th century through commerce, and was present as early as the 11th.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Hausa language and culture, despite political divisions.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses within walled compounds; millet and sorghum.

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread through traders and scholars.

colonisation.value: None; the cities were conquered by Fulani forces (the Sokoto Caliphate) in 1804–08.

riseSignals.value: Seven original Hausa states (the Hausa Bakwai), traditionally founded by the sons and grandsons of Bayajidda.

peakPeriod.value: The page says the states emerged mainly in the 16th century as powerful trading states; Muhammad Rumfa ruled Kano 1463–1499.

declineSignals.value: Constant wars and heavy taxes weakened the cities before the Fulani jihad of 1804.

outcome.value: Usuman dan Fodio’s jihad conquered the Hausa states by 1808; the Sokoto Caliphate was proclaimed in 1809. The British conquest date is not stated in the article.

overallCertainty.value: Early history from legends (the Bayajidda story).
